map.h4fact:0.event.0.description:
It seemed as if that night would never end. Standing dazed on the bare hilltop above the village, I couldn't take my eyes off the streaks of fire as they cut across Eeofol’s sky; they were too blistering to notice some of them go out and others light up. Then I realized they weren’t going out at all, even after I lowered my eyelids. The day was about to break, yet I could still only see a mishmash of dark and light strokes. 

Frederick told me never to look directly at the sun so as not to harm my eyesight, but he had never mentioned that searing light just like that could  pour down from the sky by night as well. I pressed my palms to my face and darted almost blindly down the slope toward the creek. I think I screamed. I was scared.
map.h4fact:0.event.1.description:
The water and the coolness helped. My eyesight was coming back to me, but the fear didn't go away—it felt as though that blinding flame kept scorching me inside. While I could still see, I noticed that the stars whose tails blazed so brightly in the night sky were not burning up in midair. They were making it all the way to the ground, like huge smoldering rocks, strangely slowly, and seemingly not far from here, just beyond those hills. Then the wind brought a faint odor of smoke—not like the morning smell of stoves in the houses.

Over the past few years, I had gotten used to asking questions, then unlearned to do it, and eventually mastered this art again. When I met a man who knew far more about the world than I could imagine, I wanted to ask and ask and ask without end—I was curious about everything. Then I suddenly realized I was asking too much nonsense. Frederick tried not to show it, but his displeasure sometimes got the best of him and he sent me away. 

There was no punishment worse than coming back from a lab with all the wonders to a barn filled with broken rakes and dirty burlap bags. I began to think before opening my mouth—and I guess I slowly learned to ask the right questions. One such question was boiling inside my head right now: Can rocks so much like the sun fall from the sky?
map.h4fact:0.event.2.description:
Find Frederick. I had to find Frederick. Nothing could be more important now. Not even because of his telescope—whatever could fall from the sky had already done it anyway... It was just my heart telling me it’d be better to be by his side now. Any knowledge he had, even the very lore that made him so feared by my fellow villagers, could be useful today.

For as long as I could remember, I had always been alone, living in the barn owned by Grampa Haye. He was not my real grandfather—that much I knew somehow, but he still fed me, gave me clothing, and let me sleep by the stove in his house in winter. The rest of the time, I preferred to be on my own. 

Frederick came into my life when I was... hmm, well, I don't even know how old I am now. Doesn't matter—that was the first time I ventured into the hills behind our grove. There, I saw a big new house, and next to it, one disturbingly tall man and two smaller ones, like halflings, but different, grey-skinned. Later on, I would learn that those little people were called "gremlins," and that they were not really human, but Frederick refused to answer my further questions, and I never saw the gremlins again. 

And back at that moment, perhaps out of fear of the unknown, I froze and let myself be caught—though I could've hidden in the woods from anyone. Frederick realized I wasn't the kind of person that chased him off to this neck of the woods, and he allowed me to come see him sometimes. I guess he needed some live ears to listen to his crazy hypotheses—and he didn't care that I was nothing more than a silly little girl who couldn't even count her fingers.

I would stay in the lab for weeks on end, for no one missed me in the village anyway. My thin hands were often just what Frederick needed. Sometimes he'd ask me to crawl inside a sophisticated machine to find a burst hose or check the wear on a gear. Such joy it gave me when I was able to help and the assembled mechanism began to hiss and spin—even though I hadn’t the faintest idea what was going on. He, however, always knew what was about to happen and why it should work.

Find Frederick. There was hardly anyone who could deal with the unusual around here.
map.h4fact:0.event.3.description:
Many who had not believed in the danger opened their eyes now, but there were also many who shrugged off the trouble, even though it was knocking at their door. The difference? The former had already seen what the celestial guests did to living beings, while the latter yet had to. It was too late for them to get wiser, though; I could watch from the hills as the creatures were flooding the farms we had left behind. 

For the first time in the decade passed since the last bad harvest, something bigger than a new turnip dish recipe had happened in the halflings’ lives... And I never imagined it’d carry this much sorrow. Frederick, where are you?
map.h4fact:0.event.4.description:
The nightmare came in the light of day. It was like if you wanted to wake up, you just couldn't because you were already awake. Wide awake and incredulous. Things that felt so important just a few days ago, seemed to be just gone, shrouded by fog. In the course of these days, the imaginary danger grew into a very real horror. Several villages in the north were gone, as if they had never existed—the news was brought by the lucky survivors. The stench of fires and sulfur was now everywhere, and any stirring in the bushes caused consternation.

At dawn we ran into some refugees. The halflings—one I recognized as the elder of a village half a day's journey away—were looking around in a daze, unsure of what to do.
“Uncle Kett! How did you make it here?” I called out to him. “Don’t tell me you ran here through the woods all night, straight from your farm… or did you?”
“Well, when someone starts ramming down your door, you’ll get not only out of bed, but out of your pants too! So yeah, we ran off... We need to gather people, that's what I think!” 
“Who chased you off? Were those goblins, like five years ago?”

I already knew the answer, but somehow I hoped Kett would say something else.

“Devils… with some big old horns. I don’t really know what they were," the elder said sheepishly. "They killed my dog right away… he whined so horribly. Then they kicked in the door. And I jumped out the window; no time to get dressed that was. They stood in a circle around the farm. I don't even remember how I got past them. I met someone else in the forest later. I'm afraid that's all of us, though, and we’ll never see the rest…”
map.h4fact:0.event.5.description:
I'd often been berated and branded an adventure-seeker. But what are adventures? Stories of glorious heroes and dragon slayers sung in taverns by traveling bards? Sure, I liked to listen to them—but they never mentioned the fatigue, the bloody feet, the stench of dead bodies, or the screams of people eaten alive that echoed through the forest all night. The demons were on the prowl. Villages were not enough for them—those who had taken shelter in the woods were now in danger too. Frederick and I spent the night sitting by the fire looking in the flames, regurgitating the same slow, meaningless remarks. We were so exhausted, we couldn't even bring ourselves to sleep. If that was adventure, then I can assure you I never wanted adventure.

By morning we were in agreement: nothing left to do here for us. We must leave the Valley immediately.
map.h4fact:0.event.6.description:
As the sun was getting high, the numbness we had fallen into the previous night had finally subsided. At least Frederick spoke as quickly and vigorously as before, and his eye was keenly aware of the smallest details in the chaos. 

“Henrietta, I want to thank you again. Perfect timing to get me out; it seems our aliens know more about demonology than the entire Bracadan Academy. They're already summoning some pretty powerful creatures from the Elemental Plane of Fire, and I don't see them needing months of rituals, rare reagents, or the favorable position of celestial bodies to do it. If we delay any longer… I wouldn't love to see Eeofol turned into a nice balmy place like the ones where those things are coming from, through their portals and gates. You know, some of them prefer to live in active volcanoes, and this land is full of fire-breathing mountains that once became dormant but can be brought back to life."
map.h4fact:0.event.7.description: All night long something rustled, whooshed and muttered around the camp. It was the little servants of the horned creatures—imps and familiars. We tried to scare them off by launching exploding projectiles into the darkness, but to no avail... By morning, the vile creatures were snooping around almost in plain sight, unafraid of anything. In a few more hours, this horde would overrun the last corners of our part of Eeofol. It was as clear as day: if we did not leave the Valley today, all would be lost.
map.h4fact:0.guards.12.20.0.message:
As we approached the campfire, we saw a hastily abandoned camp. The footprints of a dozen two-legged creatures led away from it into the forest. Two decapitated carcasses of celestial guests were lying by the fire—it looked like someone had begun field dressing them, but left halfway through.
“Ah, those are halflings…” you hear from the bushes. “Go away! Don't you dare follow us, or we'll have you taste steel, like we did to those freaks!”
Apparently, the men in the bushes are hardly nicer than the horned ones. Are they the same gang that brought mayhem to the neighboring valley five years ago? They’d been forgotten by now, but surely there was no way a new one would just pop up out of nowhere right here. Well, I guess trouble comes in threes.
map.h4fact:0.guards.14.12.0.message:
The horned one lies on the ground, hit between the eyes with a few heavy slingshot bullets. His head is cracked, one horn broken off. What seemed unthinkable yesterday is now sprinkling our land with its stinking blood. A beast, it would seem; but no, not a beast. His eyes were too intelligent until they faded. Not an elemental spirit, not a human, not a magic creature. And silence all around. Nothing more to argue about.

“We should inform everyone about this devilry at once!”
“How many of them are roaming the forests now, trampling our mushrooms!”
“We must prepare an ambush!” I heard from the halflings flocking around the vanquished creature. Suddenly the ruckus died down, and I felt a dozen intense stares.
“Henrietta, you've walked every path around here! You're the only one who knows shortcuts to all the places!”

What an ordeal it is for them to go beyond the outskirts of their home village. All their lives, they had been afraid of strangers, and here was their fear embodied. Even dead, it made them sweat, but right now, they stood with their chins high and spat on the brown corpse. But if there's any more out there…

“Why, lads, where there is one, there gonna be others, right? We'd better get some heavy rocks and go together!” Kosta, an elderly carter who was lamenting the horses, threw his hat on the ground. “I wanna make these singed hogs pay for my ponies! Show the way, lass—can’t we cut through the woods to Tall Ridges?”
map.h4fact:0.guards.15.13.0.message:
There was indeed a "hole" in the place the villagers had mentioned—one with smooth, seemingly melted edges, but somehow it didn't feel too hot near it, and it didn't even look like something had been burning there. What could that mean? Some of those stars that fell in the night didn't announce their imminent arrival, but simply traveled... wherever they needed to…? I froze, frightened by my thoughts, while the clamoring peasants kept waving their hands and rebuking me, as if it all were somehow my doing. I turned back to them and tried to come up with an answer; suddenly, the outrage on their faces gave way to surprise and then to horror. Stunned, I realized the villagers were looking not at me, but behind me.

A pair of sharp, crescent-shaped horns appeared above the hole's edge. Then two huge red paws followed, and finally, their owner got out of the pit with a mighty leap. Straightening up, he inhaled gurglingly and let out two streams of smoke. Huge in stature, with lumpy skin the color of fresh meat—or with no skin at all?—here, in the middle of the village, he looked infinitely alien. The eyes of the weird guest were fiery spots, and the air around his figure was churning like it does above a frying pan. 

I felt a wave of heat and a strange, iron-like odor or taste on my tongue—and then it was as if a chemical reaction had stopped, like at Frederick's, when he’d let me drop some "im-ge-be-tor" in a flask. The monster's eyes became dim, its skin turned brown, the heat around it subsided, and I could finally get a good look at it. If one were to imagine a huge wild boar growing horns, losing its bristles, standing up on two legs like a man, and growing big humps on its back and chest... that would still be a very rough and flattering description of the being I saw. Its ugliness was striking.

The creature wiggled its huge head around and looked at the crowd. Its snare-like mouth opened, and a disgustingly long tongue fell out. With a loud clang, the monster took its first step on the land of Eeofol. Funny, I thought, as if some good farrier had already shod him...
map.h4fact:0.guards.19.9.0.message:
The sign at the gate reads:
"Experimental maintenance shop. Property of the mining company. Currently not hiring."
Looking closer, I noticed scratches on the sign. Barely visible smudges of dirt complement them, forming the symbols of a secret alphabet invented by Frederick. 
"...You'll soon come rushing here, like if it smelt of hot apple pies. This starfall breaks all the laws of cosmology: I've never seen such phenomena described anywhere... the speed of passing celestial bodies, the deceleration exceeding all norms, flame streams with a vector opposite to... the strongest light filter broke... extremely interesting, but the situation forces me to leave the home. Names and faces from a past life have resurfaced; it could be dangerous. Be careful and don't forget our secret! I am heading south, and don’t even think..."
map.h4fact:0.guards.21.5.0.message:
We stepped through the door that opened before Frederick, followed by a line of halflings. None of them had ever been here before. Had it been any other time, they would have been struck by the sight of the elegant laboratory, topped by a Bracadan-style dome; they hadn’t seen anything much nicer than plain stone huts and wooden barns. But no, the villagers had had enough shocks over the last few days, and the only thing they were looking for was a chance to plop down on the grass and give their tired feet a good rubbing. We decided not to disturb the weary halflings yet and first headed up the hill so that Frederick could check on his creations being prepared for their first big flight. 

The sight was incredible! In the middle of a clearing surrounded by snow-capped mountains, three huge bubbles were swaying majestically in the wind, with a very large boat beneath each one. 

I confess: even I gaped at the sight of the spider-like mechanisms moving deftly about the decks and tackle, tightening knots with their steel beaks and doing something else totally incomprehensible. Soon Frederick was back from his inspection of those, as he called them, airships. With a hint of pride in his voice, he said:

“A job well done! My automatons are working smoothly and without error. The tanks are filled to the top with water. All that's left is to put the orbs of fire in the furnaces, and we're ready to go! I'll steer the main airship, and the mechanical assistants will repeat my maneuvers on the others.”

We went back to the halflings. The peaceful scenery of the valley nested between the mountains seemed to have calmed the poor villagers—perhaps even a bit too much. Some were asleep, while others were lighting their pipes. Frederick shook his head, grabbed a tin cone, and spoke into its top. The thing made his voice so loud that those who were resting leapt up. 

“Enough sleeping! Go, go, let's get a move on! Time is very, very short: the demons may appear any minute now, and then we will all be in big trouble. In the building in front of you there are supplies prepared—not a lot, but better than nothing. Take the crates and carry them where I show you, if you don't want to starve to death during the journey.”
“Hope those lazies didn’t forget the sack..." Frederick said with the cone out of his face, and I was the only one who heard him. 

Suddenly, someone touched my shoulder. I turned around and met Tavin's gaze. He emerged silently behind me—but that was to be expected of a veteran like him. I wanted to greet him, glad that the Guard had survived, but there was something in his eyes that made me hesitate. Tavin squinted at me and said:

“If I had no trouble tracking down and finding you, those infernal beasts will do no worse. They've got as good a nose as the best hunting dogs in Erathia. Give me a week’s worth of provisions and a sack of those firecrackers. I'll lead them away from the valley. At the very least, I'll buy you some time, holding them back for a bit.”
“But… Tavin, what are you talking about? We need you and your expertise! It would be suicide to go up against those beasts alone. Maybe they won't yet find the secret passage.” 
“Don't try to change my mind, child. If my life saves hundreds of yours, that's the price I'll pay. That's why I became a soldier. Someday you'll understand.” 

I sighed and, feeling weak in my legs, did as he asked. Tavin slung the sack on his shoulder, looked me in the eye again, and, without another word or a glance back, he strode firmly out of the valley.
map.h4fact:0.guards.23.18.0.message:
The ragged cohort lined up for battle. Commands were heard, but no longer in Erathian. Some alien tongue, crude and animalistic. Shields and surcoats over their armor were thickly stained with blood—they didn’t even attempt to clean them. How could they dare to betray? To submit to this vile force? What had broken the will of these seasoned soldiers—was it the fear of imminent death... or of being turned into alien flesh?

It doesn't matter now. There is only one way north.
map.h4fact:0.guards.23.24.0.message:
A palisade was an unusual sight for these places, yet someone had cared enough to build it. That gave me some hope, even if faint. The sentries were steady and waved cheerfully, inviting me to enter the camp.
My companions fell to the ground right as we stepped inside the walls; several days with barely any food or proper rest had taken their toll on them. They were unaccustomed to such deprivation of their fleshy, well-fed bodies. I headed straight to meet the commander. He was standing in the center of the camp, giving instructions and waiting to talk to the new arrivals.
map.h4fact:0.guards.23.31.0.message:
“You're alive!”

“Yes, I'm alive, and I'd very much like to know which Bracadian demonologist I’ve pissed off. I've never even crossed paths with any. What a mistake.”
I didn't know what Frederick was talking about, but I was so happy to see him alive, I didn't even try to ask him anything. He, as usual, kept feeding me a mountain of thoughts and assumptions, as if I'd shown up at his lab in the morning and he couldn't wait to have my ear and share what he had cooking in his head...

“Some time ago I received a letter personally signed by Khazandar—I think I told you about him... the freest mind in Bracada, for which he will surely pay sooner or later. I had not heard of him since I left those lands, but a few years ago a messenger from him found me, and we entered into correspondence. It seemed as though our connection had been discovered un time. 

The signature in his last message looked forged to me; I decided that if I had been found indeed, I should act first. The letter proposed a meeting; Khazandar was supposedly going to send me a crucial component for a certain experiment... but there were demons waiting for me in Dry Ryehill—those are creatures from another plane of existence, you just saw them! Somebody summoned them but neglected control, so they captured me, slaughtering half the village meanwhile!"

“Frederick… those things… they weren't summoned. Or, at least, not by the wizards certainly.”

“Not by the wizards? What makes you say that? Those were some archetypal demons—I'd seen stuffed ones in the Academy’s museum!”

“Shooting stars. They came out of the rocks that fell from the sky that night.”

Frederick’s face fell; he began arguing, but I just took him to the place where the creatures were doing their ritual, and I showed him the huge crater at the village’s edge; the stone that had fallen there was so big that a devil could fit inside, maybe even a few. The rock had split open, and the cracks revealed something strange and unnatural. Either a tangle of angular pipes, or...

“Well, I’ll be— If only alchemists Widman and Statten would have seen that! I don't even want to think about… I mean, I suspected it was not a real meteor shower. Wait, so it was all a coincidence? Was Khazandar’s messenger actually waiting for me? And now you're telling me those things have already taken over half the Valley?! Henrietta, we need to get back to my lab! You go straight there right now, and I'll—I didn't tell you this, but Khazandar had once talked me into joining an interesting project, so I'd set up another research site in the mountains to the east. I need to get there now, and you…”

“I'm heading straight north. You weren't held here alone. Another prisoner said there's a detachment of Erathian soldiers camped nearby. Apparently, someone escaped the Valley and was able to call them for help. Refugees are flocking to them now. Frederick, listen! I know you don't much like halflings. Sure, I myself feel like a stranger in my own homeland sometimes—but I've seen what the monsters are up to. We have to do something or they'll kill everyone and turn them into their filthy flesh. If we don't try to save someone—well, that’ll kill me.”

“...Yeah, well, there might not be enough hands... in fact, that would be most helpful. Yes! Ahem. That's right, we can't just stay aside! Now listen: take everyone you can to my lab. Three hundred, maybe five if I can get those old Gavin’s underpants back up in the air too... Someone’s gotta help me settle down when our flight ends.“

“Flight? Are we gonna fly like birds?”

“Not exactly, but it's our only chance if the devils continue to destroy everything in their path with such abandon. Trust me as you always have, and you'll soon see it yourself. That’s it, then! I'm going to the mountains.”
map.h4fact:0.guards.26.12.0.message:
I love discovering new things, but I hate surprises. That's the beauty of the process: developing a theory and then practicing it to achieve exactly what you expect. The theory, of course, can be as bold as you like...

That unusual starfall could not help but attract my attention, even though I was thinking about other things that night. I'm not ashamed to admit that the unraveling of this phenomenon was the most unpleasant surprise in my life. All of us, the scientists of Enroth, even those who do not yet know what has happened, have been confronted with a fact: rocks can indeed fall from the sky. And not just fall, but carry guests that no one would willingly invite into their home.
 
Now I think: what if they are not rocks at all, but something akin to our airships, only more complex and perfect—or maybe only fragments of such a ship that has crashed? Is it possible that up there, so high that we can't see it even with telescopes, town-sized hulks crafted by someone are flying somewhere on their business, carrying whole nations, exchanging signals and sometimes even volleys of monstrous guns? And where do they dock—for their harbor surely cannot be on our planet, can it?

I caught myself thinking. What I would like most of all now is to find a common language with one of the aliens, to listen to their stories about their native places, to ask a thousand questions... for some reason they didn't throw me straight into the cauldron where they made their warriors from the dead flesh. Maybe they saw in me someone with whom they could reach an understanding and agree on something? Maybe I should have...

Deep in thought, I didn't notice we'd reached my old lab. Hearing Henrietta's command, "Ready the crackers!", I looked up to see a large group of aliens blocking our way. This time they were lined up in a sort of battle formation, and there was a clear leader among them, a lean, scarlet-skinned horned one clad in black armor, as if covered in a thick layer of soot. He stepped forward, looked me straight in the eye... and scraped a claw across his throat, licking his thin lips.
map.h4fact:0.guards.27.32.0.message: Beyond the old gate I met a group of halflings who were hiding here from the demons.
map.h4fact:0.guards.32.19.0.message: I got three orbs of fire out of the box with the utmost care. These lightweight, smokeless heat sources would make the water in the engine boilers bubble, and the quality of steam produced thus would make my machinery work just right. For years, Sam had been urging me to move to her place and take my designs with me. It would be quieter and all the raw materials would be readily available, she insisted. Why did I ever put this off? According to the rough calculations I'd used to keep myself busy on the road, the orbs’ charge should have been enough for the long trip to Jadame. Three would surely do it for me alone, but now I had to get every ship I had up in the air at once. Had I just a little more time to prepare, I could get the heat medium condenser running and ramp up the orbs’ initial charge... Or I could just leave everything be, take to the air, and fly to safety alone and without fear of getting stranded in the middle of the ocean. No! That would mean betraying not only Henrietta, but my very dream too.
map.h4fact:0.guards.5.21.0.message:
I'd be happy like a little girl if it weren't for the circumstances. Here is our secret! This is the storeroom with the firecrackers for the New Year celebration—we set up a dry cache for them, away from the villages. Halflings are way cautious when it comes to danger and fire, so I insisted on safekeeping these things in a secluded place. Frederick would make small batches of them in his spare time, and once a year, the villagers brought themselves to curb their aversion to the scientist, for no one else could give them this beloved amusement. Each time, Frederick would get a year's worth of foodstuffs for the firecrackers; the halflings sure loved their big celebrations! 
The people of the Valley bragged that no one else had ever witnessed fiery rains quite like that, not even in Bracada, and would stop at nothing to show their neighbors up and enjoy some honest-to-goodness miracles. Frederick would grin dryly and agree that indeed, nothing like that was ever seen in Bracada.
“There, you just slip a couple coins to some dropout illusionist quack and get twice the spectacle," he muttered to himself as he carted away his hard-earned pay.

The crates contained onion-sized spheres that exploded with a deafening bang, spraying bright droplets of fire all over. Usually they were launched into the sky out of a long pipe dug into the village square like a spring pole, but now we could use them to arm a few sling-wielding halflings. These perfectly uniform projectiles worked even better for throwing than stone bullets.
map.h4fact:0.guards.5.30.0.message: On our way out of the village, a few leprechauns tagged along. These creatures don't seem to be bothered by anything—not even demons.
map.h4fact:0.guards.8.32.0.message:
Frederick's message spoke of "names and faces from the past", and he was heading south... I thus assumed that he was going to meet some old acquaintances, and if so, they could only be meeting here, in Dry Ryehill, a place where outsiders came to trade and were less shunned than in other settlements in the Valley.

A mile away from the village, it was clear already that it was gone. Those who came here hungered not only for killing, but also for razing... Or maybe it was some twisted, alien approach to creation? What if these creatures are just as happy to contemplate mounds of burnt logs as a halfling is to behold a new, lovingly painted barn? And the earth scorched to a molten crust is as dear to them as his favorite, hand-ploughed garden beds with huge carrots were to Grampa Haye?

And if they caught those who lived here by surprise... what did they do to them?
map.h4fact:0.header.description: Henrietta and Frederick must bring the Orb of Tempestuous Fire to Frederick's Laboratory. If Henrietta or Frederick are defeated, you will lose the scenario. Your heroes are limited to level 6, but Henrietta and Frederick will bring the Charm of Mana and the Collar of Conjuring to the next scenario.
map.h4fact:0.header.name: World on Fire
map.h4fact:0.header.rumor.0.text: I’ve never seen so many shooting stars as today!
map.h4fact:0.header.rumor.1.text: It seems that demons have returned! Have you heard? They burned down some villages in the south!
map.h4fact:0.header.rumor.2.text: They say a necromancer has made his home in our land.
map.h4fact:0.header.rumor.3.text: Several days ago some wizards visited our tavern! They spent a while asking around about someone, and then headed to the mountains.
map.h4fact:0.header.rumor.4.text: They say iron spiders dwell in the mountains! I swear they were created by the mad wizard who made his home near our village.
map.h4fact:0.header.rumor.5.text: The legends warned us about this! The end is nigh!
map.h4fact:0.header.rumor.6.text: If there’s anyone who can stop the devils, it’s our giant neighbours—titans and dragons.
map.h4fact:0.heroes.5.name: Xarfax
map.h4fact:0.monster.1.25.0.message:
No one seemed to heed me in this house. The old woman was laying the table, and the children were playing by the hearth.

“Did that Feredrich put you up to this kind of follies? Don't you trust that devil! What's he doing at the graveyard? Casts spells on dug-up graves? You'll be lost with him, just like your good-for-nothing mother. Tut, tut. Hey… ya sit down and have a meal with us—can’t let a guest go hungry now, can I? There's not much, just steamed turnips—but still a dinner. Just don't think of sweet-talking us into your silliness. We're not going anywhere, no reason to. Got plenty to do.”

I realized words were useless, but I didn't refuse a snack. The old woman had mentioned something about my mother, but I didn't remember her, and no one had ever told me a word about her. I tried to get the hostess to talk over the meal—but the harridan pretended to be deaf.
map.h4fact:0.monster.10.21.0.message: Oh, can't believe it: finally, some familiar faces! We went to scoop up saltpeter water in the morning to fertilize the gardens, and there were those horned beasts—we barely got away! Let's team up...
map.h4fact:0.monster.11.32.0.message:
On our way, I tried to entertain myself in some way to avoid succumbing to horror and despondency. I painted in my mind a picture of a stern smith shoeing the screaming horned creatures. The reality turned out to be far beyond anything I could have imagined; there, in the middle of what had once been the village square of Dry Ryehill, I saw… him.

The word "devil" came to mind, for according to the drunken monk whose ranting I had once listened to in the local tavern, there was nothing more horrible than the devil, either in this world or the other. The top of the two-legged creature's head, crowned with twisted horns, was visible even over the roofs; each clawed foot seemed capable of easily covering and crushing a halfling; and a scythe that could surely cut down a whole young grove glistened in its hands. That was when I realized: the horned ones have no farriers. The devil just wags his finger at them, and they rush to shoe each other, or even themselves, fighting over hammers and nails.

Apparently what I had seen disturbed my mind; I tried to stay on the edge of madness, while it threw more and more absurd visions at me. My companions told me later that I was laughing and shouting "get some longer, sharper nails!" as they dragged me into the bushes away from the road.

“There, there, lassie,” Kosta muttered, trying to calm me down. “Sure, that’s a big beastie, yeah, a foul one—but wait till I ll hit it square in the eye with the cracker, and then we'll see who’s got the reddest nose in this village! Empty your pouches, lads! We'll teach the devil how to celebrate the New Year our way!”
map.h4fact:0.monster.12.18.0.message: These creatures looked simpler than the one in the pit—they had no metal ornaments on their paws, and only sported a single horn, thick and short. They exchanged jerky guttural noises, as if barking at each other, but I could see they understood each other much better than dogs. As soon as the pack spotted us, however, the quarreling stopped. Their hooves dug up the ground, and the vile beings rushed into the fight.
map.h4fact:0.monster.14.26.0.message: I think I lost my mind, thinking we could handle this gang of demons. I realized too late that my impulse had been madness; they spotted us, and it was too late to run...
map.h4fact:0.monster.15.20.0.message:
We followed the tracks, and presently they led us to a clearing where some ragged men were stomping about. They looked like brigands, and they could hardly have been anything else. They were hastily gathering up their belongings.

A lanky, scraggly man was explaining something to the leader, dressed a bit nicer than the others. The tall man turned at the noise and shouted, pointing his finger at us. The ringleader nodded and drew his sword.
“I told you!" the lanky one shouted, "You shouldn’t have come after us!”
map.h4fact:0.monster.16.31.0.message:
After the battle against the devil, we searched every corner of Dry Ryehill. I feared that Frederick's burned and mangled body was about to emerge from the rubble. However, we found no corpses in the village, but we saw many tracks, as if the owners of the big hooves were dragging something behind them. The tracks led to the eastern outskirts of the village, and the nearby forest had been burned to the ground.

Suddenly, swerving between the black, ugly dead trees, a small group of halflings came running straight at us.

“There! There!..” They shrieked, running at a steady gallop. I managed to catch a ginger boy with a crazy look in his eyes, and my companions grabbed the others. The redhead caught his breath and blurted out:
“They took our folk, and now they're executing them, and not to death, even worse! Help, good people, don't let the wicked do such a thing! This is a fate worse than death, worse than anything in the world…” He burst into tears.
map.h4fact:0.monster.17.12.0.message:
“It fell from the sky, can you believe it? I saw it myself! There it is, in the hole. Too scary to approach.”
“I don't see no hole in the sky. Are you seeing things, brother?”
map.h4fact:0.monster.17.15.0.message: “Whatta boom! I swear, my shutters hit the wall and came to bits....”
map.h4fact:0.monster.18.13.0.message:
“What are you doing here, wench? Heard you like to look at weird things, so go over there... Like the look of it? Eh? Struts about the place all the time, never once looks what’s at her feet; nay, likes staring at the sky way more, and now there's a gift fell down from there... Remember the hitchrail over there? Now it’s a hole in the ground as big as a gate where it was, and the ponies are all gone…”
“She and her sorceror brought us bad fortune!.. Not even old Aiker remembers anything fall from up there, and he’s old enough to have seen a living giant... if the old buzzard isn’t making it up...”
“It’s black magic, that’s what I’m saying! The evil one reached up from his mountain with his magicks and tore off a piece of the firmament! Lucky no one got hurt…”
map.h4fact:0.monster.21.32.0.message:
The wind blew a pall of stinking smoke in our direction. With it, a great, desperate, almost inhuman shriek came to us, and then we heard an eerie, rumbling voice, which seemed to be coming from beneath the ground. We rushed into the smoke, and after a hundred paces we saw a picture that made our eyes water.

In the middle of what once was a meadow, now just a circle of scorched earth, there stood something like a huge hearth with a flat stone cauldron, its walls red-hot, and around it, a lake of thick fire slurry was glowing and gurgling. Knee-deep in it, as if ignorant of the heat, tall, mighty creatures with bright red skin were standing, and a few more giants of the same kind were driving a flock of stumbling halflings to the cauldron with their long whips. Farther away, near the burned trees, some horned beasts, already familiar to us, were standing guard over a large crowd of villagers.

The halflings were brought to the cauldron, and among them I recognized Maltman, the innkeeper from Dry Ryehill. Before I knew it, the red giant had swung his whip in a fiery arc, and three unfortunates fell dead. The crowd began shrieking again, while the monsters seemed to be doing their usual, enjoyable work—tossing corpses to each other, easily tearing them limb from limb, throwing them into the cauldron... One of the creatures looked inside; then, apparently satisfied, it made a sign to the others. The giants stared at the cauldron, gestured with their hands some, roared, and their eyes glowed. Then, the voice we had heard from afar sounded again, as if the hell itself had spoken! The flesh of the executed instantly burst into flames, turned into a disgusting mash, boiled up into a huge cap of brown foam, and fell; in the midst of the cauldron, the ugly figure of a one-horned monster appeared. Its body was billowing smoke, and the drying sludge dripped down its body with a hiss.

The ginger boy was right; fate worse than death exists now.
map.h4fact:0.monster.22.22.0.message:
Everyone in Eeofol had heard of Tavin—but not everyone spoke of him favorably. The halfling who left his home village of his own free will to join the Erathian border guards was hardly a role model they wanted for their children. Years of military service had left visible marks on the commander's hard face—his faded eyes were deeply sunken, his nose was broken, and his leathery cheek twitched distressingly every now and then.

“What's going on north?” Tavin asked, wasting no time on greetings.
“I have death at my heels. We've broken away, but the villagers…”
"Good as dead," the commander snapped. “The woods here are already crawling with creatures, and any day now they will be under every bush. In the south and west, everyone who didn't escape has already been turned into meat. I led the advance party of the Guards, followed by the rest of the men under Captain Xarfax's command, a half-day’s march behind us.”
“Followed? Were they attacked by the horned beasts on their way?”
“No, they came just fine. There's only one way out of here, but that's where they're standing now... just them. I served with Xarfax for 15 years. And today, when I went to rendezvous with his unit, he ordered his men to cut out my liver. We barely got away and hid behind those flimsy walls. Now we're figuring out how to make ourselves tasty so the devils don't get bored eating us.”
“Tavin, we need to get through. There's still hope of rescuing someone, but we need to get to the north road. Your commander is a traitor, but together we can...”
Tavin grabbed me by the collar with a snarl and yanked me into the air like a sack of rags. His gaze was frightening.
“Fool! Stupid girl! Xarfax did not betray. The devils bewitched him, you hear that?! You're going to take your dolts with the firecrackers and we're going to beat this foolishness out of the old man! And then you're going to grab whoever you can… and go do what you're gonna do. I don't want to know about it, so I won't tell anything when they catch me and start roasting me over a slow fire like a Bluemeadow sausage.”
map.h4fact:0.monster.30.32.0.message: It's those horned slop buckets again, but now the first move is mine! Hah. Let's see what you're worth when my hands are untied!
map.h4fact:0.monster.32.20.0.message:
The mages appeared suddenly, as if a veil of invisibility had fallen. Of course, I could feel their presence. These are powerful mages—their energy cannot be hidden. Very good. Even stronger ones could have taken care of that.

“Renegade Frederick!”

Their leader's voice came from all directions at once, as if from the sky. No echo, no whisper of leaves or wind, just impassive speech pouring straight into my ears.

“The Council of Bracada knows of your dark deeds: your forbidden practice of necromancy, your stealing of the skyship, your disgraceful flight from Bracada, and your ties to the renegade Khazandar. However, you have done no harm to the living and thus deserve a fair trial and a fair sentence—we will guarantee that the punishment does not include death. Lay down your weapons, release the energy from your body, and approach us. You know it full well: by following this path you have fallen into sin. The dark books may give knowledge, but it is always laced with poison of pain and death. A researcher must not spread it. You still consider yourself a seeker, don't you? Redeem yourself, Frederick, and live on as a honest man.”

My lips spread into a smile. I've heard it all too many times.

“Gods! Liston, it's you, isn't it? Still working as a heavy club in the grip of Gavin’s morality police? And you had so much potential back in the day. "Renegade Frederick" is even flattering to hear. But "renegade Khazandar"?! Isn’t that too big for your britches? Even your superiors haven't dared to decide anything regarding him yet; I would have known it otherwise. There's too much of his merit, too many other respected wizards in the Academy who won't let you dumb thugs take down the best mind in Bracada based on ridiculous speculation—and Magnus himself hasn't spoken yet. "Forbidden practices"! Do you realize how ridiculous that sounds? Tell me, former colleague... is there really a big difference between Nagas and Medusas? Oh right, the Medusas are the result of a twisted process that causes the surviving objects to rage and feel anguish. How could I forget! And gremlins differ from troglodytes only in the fact their slavery is signed by magical contracts and seals—am I not confused? Sure, everyone needs servants. And putting the souls of fallen warriors into statues to get sapient titans is, of course, fair to the dead and purely academically impeccable. Well, well, well, why blushing so much? Let's start exchanging spells. We won't ever get each other, Liston. Your mind is not free…”
map.h4fact:0.monster.34.24.0.message:
The legacy of the Time of Wonders is truly priceless. Rulers and warriors yearn to find armor and weapons dating back to those times, but they are not what matters to someone who wants to change the whole world in time. I've spent a long time gathering tiny scraps of ancient secrets to build something of my own from them... and I've gotten somewhere. My machines are still very vulnerable, their propulsion systems are unstable and inefficient, but they are reasonably autonomous and capable of making simple decisions on their own—and that's something, wouldn't you agree!

The automatons and the assembly line await!
map.h4fact:0.monster.34.34.0.message: Stopping for a second, I dug into my memory. No, there shouldn't be anything in the cemetery that would be important right now. Except for a couple of... things that might come in handy for experiments someday, but I changed my field of scientific interest quite some time ago. Not that anyone cares. Just once can you… no, it's true what they say; only the dead don't care about reputation.
map.h4fact:0.monster.7.26.0.message:
These things are already here, too! Did they really arrive on the rocks from the sky? And where are the blacksmiths who forged their horseshoes? Are those coming next?

The monsters split into groups, as if planning to pincer me and my companions. They were certainly more intelligent than animals—and they were getting more and more numerous! Sure, we had our slings ready, and enough stone bullets for all of them, but I really wished we had something stronger.
map.h4fact:0.monster.9.27.0.message: The two-horned creatures were noticeably different from their lighter-skinned kin, not only in appearance but also in behavior, just like adults are different from a bunch of feckless teens. They were clearly better organized, so they spotted us earlier. The creatures quickly banded up into several squads and attacked.
map.h4fact:0.quest.1.28.0.firstVisit:
The head of the family, the honorable Odo Two Aulns, heard me out, but didn’t bat an eye.
“Your adventurousness will not do you any good, Henrietta. I think you're making it all up, but you know me,” Odo grinned, “can't say no to a young lass—I'd have some of my lads go with you, but since you say there are such horrors around, it wouldn't hurt us to protect ourselves, would it? Tell you what, get the elder of Dry Ryehill to lend us the Pendant of Dispassion, then we can stay protected and spare those men.”

map.h4fact:0.quest.14.23.0.completed: The head of the family eyes up the bag of jewels greedily, and the laborers take their slings and get ready to follow you. Do you wish to hire them?
map.h4fact:0.quest.14.23.0.firstVisit: This family lives in the sticks and remains impenetrably calm—Henrietta even thinks that the solitude and monotony of their lives have made them quite dim. When they hear the latest news, they don't even bat an eye. The gray-haired father laments the lack of manpower, but agrees to let some of his laborers go with you, yet only for a hefty payment.
map.h4fact:0.quest.14.23.0.nextVisit: The head of the family declares that his workers won’t be going anywhere for free.
map.h4fact:0.quest.22.6.0.completed: Frederick presses his palm against the lock, and it trembles. His fingers make a shape and touch the lock again, several times. Something clicks inside; the shackle, as if turned liquid, disappears inside the case. Frederick swings the gate open and invites all to follow him.
map.h4fact:0.quest.22.6.0.firstVisit: Frederick had long ago entrusted Henrietta with the key to his laboratory, but today she is surprised to find another pair of lugs on the gate, with the shackle of a ponderous lock threaded through. There is no semblance of a chink on it, and all attempts to find some secret button are futile. Its secret is probably only known to the scientist himself.
map.h4fact:0.quest.22.6.0.nextVisit: All attempts to open the heavy lock are futile. The shackle is so thick, even if one were to try sawing it off, it would take hours, perhaps even days. Even if the lock was cast in solid gold as a reward for the more persistent burglars, there is no time for such foolishness now.
map.h4fact:0.quest.23.8.0.firstVisit: This road comes down from the laboratory, and leads south through the forest towards Dry Ryehill. There's no point in going down this road now—must find Frederick.
map.h4fact:0.quest.23.8.0.nextVisit: This road comes down from the laboratory, and leads south through the forest towards Dry Ryehill. There's no point in going down this road now—must find Frederick.
map.h4fact:0.quest.24.16.0.completed: After the defeat of the possessed and the flight of Xarfax himself, this outpost was deserted. Do you want to pass?
map.h4fact:0.quest.24.16.0.firstVisit: The closed gates of the Erathian outpost can be seen ahead.

map.h4fact:1.event.1.description:
Burton stunk. That was our first impression of the place. The whole town was permeated with the acrid odor of something unfamiliar—it made the air feel heavy, sticky... and dirty, if one can say that about the air.

Because of this stench, our arrival in Jadame almost spiraled into a big scandal in the very first minutes we set feet on its land. We had been through a lot on the way, and many of us had taken the journey very hard. And still, the moment we were on solid ground and taking in the air of the new world, the Eeofolian refugees cried out as one that they hated the place, and demanded that we keep going. I had no idea what to say to them, so I just looked at Frederick. I could see how great a toll it took on him to be forced into the company of the villagers, who kept pestering him with their ill-placed complaints and requests. Now I saw his face growing purpler with every new shout from the crowd, and I knew that an outburst could not be avoided. 

However, the storm came in from an unexpected direction. From behind the scholar's back strutted a short, stout woman, her sleeves rolled up. She appeared to be his Jadamean colleague, Sam—he had told me a little about her on the way. On her face, I could see fatigue mingle with anger, and sadness with determination. She put her fists at her sides, looked Frederick in the eye, and shouted hoarsely:

“Frederick, old fella! I sure expected you to come sooner or later, and not just you; you were bound to go for it and come to lie low at the bottom of our hole! But whoa, if there isn't more of you here than armadillos on old Donald's ranch... Well, hulloa to you, dear guests. My grandfather's grandfather had spent forty years looking for a place to put down roots in this land. And you know what? He found the only place for hundreds of miles around that didn't stink. And then the Ogres came and took his head off—thank the gods that the old fool had fathered some sons by then, who scattered to the eight winds as soon as they grew up. My father's grandfather wasn’t one for grand ideas—the place where he settled stank just like everywhere else around here, but it was a good spot to fight off enemies. My father's father found out the source of the stench—see the old fountain over there? He dug a well to get water for it, but it spewed out earth oil instead. That's what makes this place reek. My father figured out that the oil burned well, so he learned how to smelt metal with this nasty, hot fuel. And then some Ogre lads came here from places where it doesn't stink indeed, but one can't get metal for weapons and armor either. Guess what they offered him?”

“Uh, to trade the metal for something they had a lot of?” suggested one of the halflings.

“Atta boy! You got it! And you know what ogres have a lot of? Dumb brawn. Their bigwig went and smashed my dad into a puddle with his club and then said we'd better give up all the metal, so they wouldn't kill anymore in return. Maybe. Well, at least not all of us. Perhaps. If the mood strikes. Probably not, though. Anyway, he'd done a stellar job of encouraging us. Oh, by the way, lookie there, and there, and over there,” Sam made a full circle with her hand, pointing to the outskirts of the town. "Those good ol’ Ogre boys are everywhere. And over there, in a spot where it doesn't stink, lies their main fortress, where there sits one fat, slimy toad, looks like fresh armadillo crap, goes by Zog. Yeah, and there are several hundred more of his jolly good chums there. Wanna keep going? I'm not gonna beg you not to. But I can see your bubbles won't last more than a hundred miles without repairs, with all the holes and whatnot. Where you'll have to land next time, I won't even guess. Well, I hope it won’t stink here. Good riddance.”
map.h4fact:1.event.10.description:
For some time the sky had been a source of anxiety rather than admiration for me, yet I couldn't help but recognize that it looked particularly beautiful tonight. The myriad of stars above the moonlit stone valleys glittered like finely cut gems, only found in the treasuries of the richest princes. I must confess: I shamelessly lifted this beautiful comparison from one of the novels Frederick had almost used as fuel, lamenting having this "ballast" in his hastily packed luggage instead of some more useful reference books. 

I hadn't ever seen any of those gems myself, of course, but I couldn't have said it better myself. Sam and I sat around the fire, roasting skewered meat and bread, and I listened avidly to her incredible stories. Sam seemed to have as many of them as the stars above us. I had a couple of amusing tales from village life to tell myself, too, and Sam enjoyed them well enough, choking back a hoarse laugh every now and then. I seemed to have made a first new friend in a very long time. Frederick didn't take part in our conversation—he was busy with some research of his own. He had brought a whole crateload of mirrors, tubes, curved rulers, and other instruments to the fire, but spent most of the evening in the darkness a ways aside, occasionally running up and grabbing new glass pieces and devices. 

Sam and I watched for a while as Frederick surveyed the sky through a long pipe, like those he said seafarers used on ships to see distant land, but it wasn't too much fun, so we went back to our chat. When all the meat had been eaten and only embers remained of the fire, Frederick returned and raised a finger. Mysteriously illuminated by the faint flicker of the campfire, he said: 

“The moon! They are from the moon!”

“Who?” I asked.

“The demons. It all adds up: they live on the moon. That’s scarcely a surprise; too many dark cults and practices are associated with this luminary. Every scientist and navigator knows: our world is shaped like a sphere, and the luminaries orbit around it, giving us sunlight by day and moonlight at night. Academic science believes that only incorporeal creatures can dwell on the Sun and the Moon. There are other hypotheses, but when choosing between the improbable and the absolutely improbable, I always end up leaning towards the more down-to-earth explanation. I have been looking at the Moon through a telescope for a very long time. I am sure now that what I have been able to make out are mountains, plains and countless craters, which means that the places I see are material. The demons probably built their own cities and castles there—and surely, they were watching our world below, perhaps through a spyglass just like mine. Full of jealousy of our blue oceans, our green forests and vast meadows, they were preparing an invasion, and that night, their stone ships rained down on Eeofol, turning the fertile land into an ash-filled desert akin to the one from which they came. Those were ships—there is no doubt about that. When I looked into the cracks, I saw something there—probably not mechanisms... or mechanisms operating on principles unknown to me, but most definitely products of the mind rather than natural formations.”

That night I slept badly—I dreamt of the devils again. They tore up trees, crushed mountains into rubble with their bare hands, and stacked the rocks up into huge, ugly towers. Is there any power that can resist this?
map.h4fact:1.event.11.description:
I watched Burton prepare to come face to face with Zog. Yesterday's plowmen and shepherds, the halflings were hastily learning the craft of war. Most of my countrymen are good shots with a sling, but we'd never had to practice on dirtskin-like dummies or fire volleys on command before. Hopefully, when the time comes, real bombs will hit real ogres with the same accuracy. I tried discussing the preparations with Frederick, only to find him completely serene. I only ever saw him so impassive during crucial experiments or the launching of a fancy new machine. 

“Frederick, do we have a chance of defeating Zog?”

“While Zog and his chums are nested up in their fortress, picking their noses with clubs, more and more batches of battle-ready automatons are coming out of our workshops. We're going to give this savage a nasty surprise. Even if he expects to meet resistance, he's probably imagining something like a bunch of barely trained women and midgets, hardly capable of giving him any trouble.” I decided to take no offense at Frederick for comparing halflings to midgets.  

“You know, that's good, but I wouldn't say it makes me feel much better. Zog doesn't see us as a threat, sure, but we too only have a vague idea of what we will be in for once we get to his lair. The scouts are doing their best, but they have little experience and even less reliable information. We need more scouts, more spyglasses. New ones, better than the ones we have.”

“You're a smart girl, Henrietta, and I'm glad I wasn't wrong in thinking you were a quick learner. Caught off guard by demons once, you're now doing your best to learn everything you can about your enemy before you meet him face to face. I have already thought about how to improve the spyglasses to make them handier for the halflings. A shorter focal length at the same magnification factor, compact size... Not too mention that your talent for silent walking and short stature will allow you to infiltrate deeper into enemy territory than Sam's scouts can. Can you find any capable halflings ready for such an endeavor?” 

“Yes," I answered calmly enough. Without ever meaning to, I'd been gaining experience in leading my brethren since the first day of the invasion, and I was really getting the hang of it.
map.h4fact:1.event.12.description:
“Frederick, how much longer should our preparations take?” I asked.

“The enemy is a serious one, so the preparations should be just as serious, my little friend.”

“But the scouts report that Zog has already caught wind of our growing strength. He's about to leave his lair; either he’ll bring the fight to us on his own terms or may very well run away! We must pin him down in his fortress where he has no chance to retreat or escape!”
map.h4fact:1.event.13.description:
"Girl, the only thing ogres respect is strength. I mean, you can even get along with a dirtskin—provided you first break his face, then drag him through the mud in front of a crowd, so that everyone knows you are stronger than him, and that it would be no great shame for him to yield to you. Then he'll become your doormat, and only then you'll know he's no longer a danger to you... but, most likely, this will not last either. You see, there are no equals among the ogres; they only have a pecking order—like the Rocs. Whoever has a nest on the cliff higher up can crap on everyone below. And the one who is being crapped on dreams of moving to the very top and taking revenge on everyone who used to be above him."

"Well, suppose we rough up the one who nests at the very top... That place where it doesn't stink. Maybe then they'll be more cooperative—eh, Sam?"

"Well... we can try, of course, but I wouldn't have high hopes that it'd solve our problem once and for all. I think you'll find out soon enough. What did your jokester pals say? A halfling is not who?.. So: an ogre is not a bird either, heh, heh... but if you kick him hard enough, he'll grow some wings to flap and might even try to lay some eggs... Anyway, if we are to get to Zog, we'll have to put these mugs at our service—after we give them a thorough beating, of course. With any luck, we'll then sort out our troubles before they remember that an ogre is not a bird and shouldn't be living in a coop. And you certainly can't rely on them freaks when we go balls to the wall. The only ones you should trust are your lads with slings, the ones who know what they owe you and what's at stake. And you can always count on our burners, too..."
map.h4fact:1.event.2.description:
The refugees stood there, their faces paper white. Those who had begun climbing the gangways back to the ships froze between sky and earth, clinging to the steps. I took a deep breath, making an effort not to cringe from the smell, picked at the red earth with my toe... and stepped forward.

“Hello, Sam. I realize you were expecting Frederick and his friends and never thought there would be so many of us—but we've all lost our home. If you let us stay here, we'll be grateful and try to make ourselves useful. We don’t shy away from working... or fighting.”

At my last words, the faces of the halflings around me fell, but, thank the gods, no one blurted out a peep. Surprisingly, Sam's speech somehow calmed them down and cheered them up at the same time: they all silently rushed to unload the airships.

When the hard work was done, Sam invited everyone to the hastily set tables. There was unknown, suspiciously smelling meat giving off lots of steam, and quite a few bottles of wine; oddly greenish in hue, yet still undeniably wine. Hot food finally wiped away the fatigue of the grueling flight. Some of us, who had maybe developed a bit too much of an appreciation for the local libation, even began cracking jokes along the lines of, "Sure, halfling is not a bird, but..."
map.h4fact:1.event.3.description:
The town made a strong impression, though a mixed one. There were… big houses? Small factories? Something in-between the two, all over the place. Smoke, steam, creaking wood and clanking metal... Nothing like our quiet, tidy villages, but I felt my compatriots would settle in quickly. There was no way out, and if a halfling put down roots somewhere, it would soon bound to become a cozy home, even if it had to start with a burrow under a mountain. We didn't have to dig, though—Sam had quartered the refugees in old adobes on the outskirts. 

They had been built many years ago by a small tribe of ogres who had quarreled with their kin and come begging to be hired as laborers, but in the end the giants proved incapable of doing useful work and drifted away, never to be heard from again. Their dwellings had stood decaying ever since, and they were about to be taken apart for stone, before they suddenly came in handy. The little halflings thought these structures huge and uncomfortable, but only at first. In a couple of days the walls were lined with all kinds of potted tomatoes and other plants, and Urstan, the village carpenter, was busy crafting elegant tables and chairs to fit the new dwellers.

The locals, the mechanics, turned out to be people of few words, but awe-inspiringly hardworking. Even most children here were well-accustomed to getting up early and helping the adults in their shops or forges instead of horsing around and playing. Sam turned out to have a wealth of organizational talent—the very next day each halfling had been issued a leather apron with a set of simple tools and instructed on the work to be done. 

Labor is the best remedy for sad thoughts. Before I knew it, Sam's new apprentices were up to their ears in the production of all sorts of mechanical parts: gears, bushings, shafts, cams, and things of whose purpose I had not the slightest idea; I had only ever seen them piled up in a workshop in distant Eeofol. Like, what is a nozzle valve and what is it for? I could have asked Frederick, of course, but I didn't dare to distract him now. He was busy erecting an enormous hangar, or shed, or whatever on the edge of the village, seeing as our airships were in need of a thorough overhaul. Provided, of course, just an overhaul would be enough...

The lull didn't last long; one of Sam's scouts brought word that an army led by one of Zog's lieutenants had moved out towards Burton, and that they would be here soon. The locals didn't seem to be fazed by the news, but the clanging, clanking, and scraping in the shops grew louder, and the town sank into a heavy mixture of steam and smoke.
map.h4fact:1.event.4.description:
The day came when I finally learned where this odd-tasting, tough meat came from...

Those creatures, looking like moving piles of stones with short, thick legs, served not only as a source of food but also as pack animals. Awfully stubborn, but calm and plodding, they grazed peacefully in large fenced areas—I thought them completely barren, but, apparently, there was some fodder to be found there. They were what the locals called armadillos. Each herd had a leader with a huge bony collar, and it seemed to me that those big guys demanded special treatment. However, my old acquaintance Kosta didn't even seem to be bothered by the fact that his new friends sported neither hooves nor braided manes. Within a couple of days after our arrival I saw him bumbling around the stalls, peeking into the mouths of those huge armadillo beasts, harnessing them and generally looking absolutely happy. I wish I could be like that. I haven't found me the right thing to do here yet.
map.h4fact:1.event.5.description:
A week passed since we had settled in Jadame.

Burton and its outskirts were not very green at all, and there were no ponds, just black puddles of bubbling sludge; they gave off that trademark stench, to which, however, we became accustomed after a week or so. The local boys would sometimes set fire to one as a prank, for which they’d get a good slapping from their mothers—and the local women, it must be mentioned, could easily chuck a blacksmith's hammer several fathoms up with one hand. No wonder the naughty kids would lose their will to quarrel at the mere sight of their mothers frowning.

I had been hesitating to ask Sam this for a while; finally, I got myself together and inquired why there were so few men in Burton, and why the women were not doing housework but rather forging, drilling, and welding metal.

“Men always think it's all in their hands! That's why we have it like this now. When the ogres began popping up in our land, they set up a kind of militia—made themselves swords, shields, muskets and whatnot. Of course, no one knew how to fight. And so they were getting killed off—one by one, one by one, and some even ended up being taken as slaves to Zog.
Well, to speak the truth, our women didn't have much women's work to do even before that. You can see that nothing really grows here in our land. There's only earth oil, ore, and weeds, which only armadillos can stomach, so all we had to do was take care of the cattle. An armadillo is not a sheep or a cow, mind you, and it's not that easy to handle. Takes some strength and will. Doesn't really take a lot of shepherding, though, so we helped our fathers and husbands, learning how to forge, cast metal, do everything. Now it has come to the point that there are almost no men left at all... oh, well, somehow we manage. We can't give up. If we have goods, we have at least something to trade for food at the port market in Orca's Maw. But we can't get there now, on account of the dirtskins blocking the road our caravans take. They know we've got something to surprise them down here, so they don't dare take on us yet, but if we can't drive them back to their non-stinking hole in the mountains before long, they'll take us by force.”

It was still a fairly quiet life in Burton, except for the noise and rumbling of the forges that most every house here had.

The halflings, to my amazement, began exploring the wastelands and even climbing small rocks in their spare time, never straying far from Burton, though.
The locals, with the exception of the scouts, were also trying to stay close, not in the least part because of the proximity of Zog's strongholds. Most of the local ogre chieftains had sworn an oath to him. While before, as per the townsfolk, at least some of them could be dealt with, cautiously enough, now the Jackal had something that made them yearn to serve him. It was rumored that recently, instead of a club adorned with a pair of stone ram horns, a sign of belonging to the noble caste of battle mages, he began to carry a huge, obviously enchanted hammer.
map.h4fact:1.event.6.description:
I had lost track of Frederick in all the hustle and bustle. There was so much to do—I mean, we were trying to make ourselves a new home and prepare to fight off Zog's ogres at the same time. I met my mentor by accident, coming out of a local forge. He wouldn't have even noticed me—burdened with a huge pile of scrolls and papers, he was waddling almost at random, and I would have missed him too, if not for the inherent ability of halflings to recognize each other, and not only, by the feet. There was no other pair of such dapper saffian boots to be found in Burton. I remember him saying, with a sad smile, that the charm for wearproof soles was the most valuable thing his Bracadan mentor had imparted on him.

“Frederick!” I called out.

“Ah, Henrietta! Been a while. I hear the refugees have been resettled. What do you think of the ogre adobes? Nice, aren't they? As we flew on, I did my best to talk myself into accepting the necessity of letting the balloons’ sailcloth go into building a tent camp—but isn't that amazing luck! All these empty, huge buildings to fit everyone in. I always thought those stories about the halflings’ exceptional luck an exaggeration, especially seeing you wreak havoc in my lab time after time. But the last few days have made even a skeptic like me a believer.”

“Yeah... The adobes are huge, but I don't know what's worse—a stuffy hole with insufferable in-laws or a hundred residents all in one place. The others seem to like the feel of their neighbor's shoulder, though even if it pushes against their ribs. It gives them some strength.”

“What about you? Isn't that why you ran away from home and found that hideout of mine even experienced Bracadan clairvoyants couldn't track down? Well, there are plenty of prying eyes in Burton now, and you know how I prefer to work when I have space and no one nosing around. I like to be face to face with my studies. That's where we're alike, Henrietta, and that's what I found intriguing in you. A curious halfling who hates to sit around in her burrow and craves for knowledge. Alright, care to give me a hand in my workshop today?”

“Oh, can I?“

I spent the rest of the day helping Frederick. We talked about a lot of things, and for the first time since our arrival, I felt warmer.
map.h4fact:1.event.7.description:
Three weeks have passed since we left Eeofol. We got used to sleeping in awkward places and positions, and we grew accustomed to the rumble of the forge hammers and the heat of the furnaces. Life was very hard, but it felt somehow as if it was becoming orderly and calm again, a change even I appreciated now. For the first time, following another exhausting day, I didn't black out as soon as my head touched the makeshift pillow. The days began to come back to me in reverse order—the awkward and funny moments of getting in step with Burton's unfamiliar lifestyle, the morning when Sam met us. 

Every day and every night of our grueling flight. I remembered being struck by the sight of the vast ocean separating Antagarich and Jadame; meanwhile, most of the halflings were so exhausted, they couldn't even begin to appreciate the breathtaking view. Waiting out the darkness, hovering over the surface of the elven lakes to give our engines rest and water. Hiding high in the clouds over the dead lands, trying to evade the huge ghost dragons, hearing their deathly howls, our hearts frozen with fear. And casting the last gaze at the receding fields and villages of our native Eeofol, almost completely obscured by smoke and the glow of fire. 

The last thing I remembered before sleep overcame me was Tavin's steely eyes, no fear in them. Just selflessness, courage and determination to hold off the demons and buy us time to escape. Oh, how we… how I need someone as fearless by my side. Could I ever become like him?
map.h4fact:1.event.8.description:
One morning, Sam barged into my place:

"It's time to go!”

“But where?”, I asked, shaking off the remnants of the dream in which I was wandering through the woods back home. Such pleasant dreams have become quite a luxury to have.

“The scouts ran into an abandoned ogre village. It seems to be the place where the dirtskins tried to set up some kind of a fair twenty years ago, before Zog became High Chieftain. Devil knows what they were going to trade in there, but whatever it was, the Jackal put a damper on it. His feel-o-sophie is, a self-respecting ogre just goes and takes what he needs when he wants it. Anyway, that's a perfect, perfect spot to set up a fortified keep! Come on, get dressed, get your boot... oh. Right. Well, just throw on some clothes, then. We move out immediately. It shouldn't take many men, but we must hurry.
map.h4fact:1.event.9.description:
The scouts found out that there indeed is a way to get into Zog's stronghold... but at what cost! There is a garrison blocking the road, hordes of bloodthirsty creatures of the most hideous kind in it... Even with the most powerful artifacts and magic, we won’t be able to avoid huge losses—and frankly, we're hardly too rich in either yet. No; we had to think of something else.
At last we had luck: a drunken ogre was spotted boasting at the campfire that his commander had an "vvvery pawafffful rrroundd stonnn", which allegedly opened a passage to a network of underground caves—there the commander met with messengers from Zog himself! Being too liberal with cactus moonshine is bad for you—especially if there may be enemy scouts nearby, catching every carelessly thrown word.
map.h4fact:1.guards.58.2.0.message: Everything indicates that you are very close to Zog's stronghold. What's more, you can smell the smoke of campfires. What if the leader of the ogres has come out of his lair to stretch his bones, hunt, collect tribute, prostrate with his backside up in front of some idol—whatever it is these scum like to do in their leisure time? No better time for a quick march and a surprise attack!
map.h4fact:1.guards.70.2.1.message: The "relic" your errant men were talking about turned out to be a magical scroll with the Teleport spell. No idea why the horned one would have hired someone, let alone this sorry bunch, to safeguard it here; however, as per one of the halflings, the minotaur had mentioned the relic should be the key to vanquishing Zog.
map.h4fact:1.header.description: To defend the town of Burton from the Ogres, you must defeat their leader Zog. If Henrietta or Frederick are defeated, the scenario will be lost. The heroes are limited to the level 12. Heroes will bring the components of the Wizard’s Well and the Ring of the Magi to the next scenario.
map.h4fact:1.header.name: Beyond the Horizon

map.h4fact:1.header.rumor.1.text: Many know there is an underground passage to Zog’s stronghold, but no one has seen it yet.
map.h4fact:1.header.rumor.2.text: Minotaurs have built their outpost northeast of Burton. It seems as though they are preparing for war against the dark dwarves.
map.h4fact:1.header.rumor.3.text: A ship flying a pirate flag has been seen in the bay near the ogres’ stronghold.
map.h4fact:1.header.rumor.4.text: A sorcerer from the lands beyond the sea settled east of Burton. They say he helps travelling mages learn new spells.
map.h4fact:1.header.rumor.5.text: Those who saw the entrance to Zog’s stronghold say it’s guarded by countless hordes of orcs and ogres.
map.h4fact:1.header.rumor.6.text: Wyverns abound in the wastelands of Ravage Roaming. A whole nest of these creatures has been spotted north of Burton!
map.h4fact:1.header.rumor.7.text: Regnan mages and artificers are hard at work developing personal firearms.
map.h4fact:1.header.rumor.8.text: The trailblazer north of Burton can help you traverse the wastelands of Ravage Roaming much faster.

map.h4fact:1.monster.24.67.0.message: So that's what the ogres look like. Huge, clumsy, with tarnished olive-colored skin, and poorly armed—but given their strength, that doesn't matter so much; a club in the hands of such a hulk can pose a greater danger than the sharpest sword. Zog seems to realize, though, that with good weapons and armor, his men would find few equals in battle. We can only hope he doesn't find another source of metal, and naturally, we won't let them get their hands on Burton craftsmanship while we're alive.
map.h4fact:1.monster.70.1.1.message:
“Halt! Who goes there?”, a menacing, but somewhat constrained voice came from the darkness.

“We are not your enemies—unless, of course, you are of Zog's gang!”

“But… What… No! We were hired to guard a sacred relic! Show yourself, you insolent stranger!”

“You?! I thought you'd been eaten by ogres!” I exclaimed, just to get hissed at from all sides. These men were the first squad we'd fielded after getting the mass production of Frederick's firecrackers up and running. They went out of town on a reconnaissance mission, but never came back. Since then, I'd been going out scouting personally.

“Hush! I'm not keen on getting buried under a cave-in! Yes, that's us. We were hired.”

“What? Hired?! As in to guard something?! I don't even want to ask by who or why. What the hell were you thinking?”

“Well… The guy was a big fella with horns and hooves, not red, though. He didn't really ask if we wanted to take him up on his offer or not, and he didn't seem to care who we were. Ridiculous, isn’t it: grenadiers in a dungeon where a boulder can drop on your head if you sneeze at the wrong time! And all because of this blasted chunk of moldy parchment! Damn it all, and may that bull-faced freak and his gold go to hell! I've forgotten what the sun looks like!” Something on the speaker’s mournful face glinted in the torchlight.

“All right, you miserable excuses for mercenaries. I forgive your defection, but now you're back in the ranks. Come on, let's get out of here! Better to die in battle than get your head caved in by a rock when you go to do a number two, innit?”
